front: What are the three constitutional elements of standing?
back: (1) Injury in fact — concrete, particularized, actual or imminent; (2) fairly traceable to the defendant's conduct; (3) likely redressed by a favorable decision. Assessed per plaintiff, per claim, per form of relief (Lujan).

front: When is a future injury sufficient for standing?
back: When it is certainly impending or there is a substantial risk it will occur; speculative chains and self-inflicted costs fail (Clapper; SBA List).

front: Does a bare statutory violation create a concrete injury?
back: No. The harm must bear a close relationship to a harm traditionally recognized by American courts (Spokeo; TransUnion).

front: Can an organization get standing by spending money to oppose a policy?
back: No. Diverting resources to oppose a policy is not an injury (FDA v. Alliance for Hippocratic Medicine, 2024).
Plaintiff's own injury + close relationship with the third party + some hindrance to the third party suing (Craig v. Boren vendor; Singleton doctor (plurality); Powers juror).
(1) Members would have standing in their own right; (2) interests germane to the organization's purpose; (3) neither claim nor relief requires individual members' participation.

front: When does a federal taxpayer have standing?
back: Only to challenge a specific congressional appropriation under the taxing and spending power as violating the Establishment Clause (Flast). Not executive spending (Hein), tax credits (Winn) or property transfers (Valley Forge).

front: Can a state sue the federal government as parens patriae for its citizens?
back: No (Massachusetts v. Mellon). It may sue for its own sovereign, quasi-sovereign or proprietary injuries (special solicitude, Massachusetts v. EPA).

front: Does an intervenor need its own Article III standing?
back: Yes, if it seeks relief different from an existing party's (Town of Chester); a party appealing alone also needs standing (Diamond v. Charles; Hollingsworth v. Perry). Ideological interest is not enough.
(1) Fitness of the issues for judicial decision; (2) hardship to the parties of withholding review (Abbott Labs).
Intention to engage in conduct arguably affected with a constitutional interest + conduct arguably proscribed + credible threat of enforcement (SBA List). No need to violate the law first (Steffel).

(1) Capable of repetition yet evading review (same party); (2) voluntary cessation unless absolutely clear it won't recur; (3) collateral consequences / live damages claims (incl. nominal); (4) certified class actions.

front: A student who challenged a school rule graduates. Is the case moot?
back: Injunctive and declaratory claims as to her are moot (DeFunis), but a damages claim (even nominal — Uzuegbunam) or expungement of discipline keeps the case alive.

front: Two most important Baker v. Carr political-question factors
back: (1) Textually demonstrable commitment of the issue to a coordinate branch; (2) lack of judicially discoverable and manageable standards.
Guarantee Clause claims; Senate impeachment-trial procedures (Nixon v. US); partisan gerrymandering (Rucho); (plurality) treaty termination (Goldwater).

front: Adequate and independent state ground — Michigan v. Long presumption
back: If a state decision fairly appears to rest primarily on federal law or is interwoven with it, the Court presumes no independent state ground unless the state court plainly says otherwise.
A federal court will not enjoin a pending state criminal prosecution (or certain civil enforcement proceedings) absent bad faith, harassment or flagrant unconstitutionality.

Bars private suits for damages/retrospective relief against a nonconsenting state or arm of the state — by its own citizens too (Hans), in state courts (Alden) and agency adjudications. Not cities or counties.

Clear waiver; valid § 5 abrogation (not Article I, except bankruptcy, war powers, eminent domain); Ex parte Young prospective relief against officers; personal-capacity damages against officers; suits by U.S. or other states.

front: Can Congress abrogate state immunity under the Commerce Clause?
back: No (Seminole Tribe). Only under § 5 of the Fourteenth Amendment, plus the plan-of-the-Convention exceptions (bankruptcy, war powers, federal eminent domain).

front: Supreme Court original jurisdiction — can Congress expand it?
back: No. Article III fixes it (ambassadors; state a party). Congress may regulate appellate jurisdiction via the Exceptions Clause (Marbury; McCardle).

front: Limits on Congress's control of jurisdiction
back: No rule of decision in a pending case without changing the law (Klein); no reopening final judgments (Plaut); no violation of independent rights or the Suspension Clause (Boumediene).
Congress may use any means rationally related (plainly adapted) to executing an enumerated power, not prohibited by the Constitution (McCulloch; Comstock). Not an independent source of power.

front: Three categories of Commerce Clause power
back: (1) Channels; (2) instrumentalities and persons/things in interstate commerce; (3) activities that substantially affect interstate commerce (Lopez).

front: When can Congress aggregate intrastate activity?
back: When the activity is economic: rational basis to conclude the aggregate substantially affects interstate commerce (Wickard; Raich). Not for noneconomic activity (Lopez; Morrison).

front: Can Congress use the Commerce Clause to compel people to buy insurance?
back: No (NFIB, Roberts opinion) — Commerce Clause regulates existing activity, not inactivity. The mandate survived as a tax.
Functional: raises some revenue, amount not prohibitive, no scienter requirement, collected by IRS through normal means → tax.

front: Dole/NFIB requirements for conditional federal grants
back: (1) General welfare; (2) unambiguous; (3) related to federal interest in the program; (4) no independent constitutional bar; (5) not coercive.
Dole: losing 5% of highway funds = mild encouragement (valid). NFIB: losing all existing Medicaid funds (>10% of state budget) = gun to the head (coercive).
Congress may enforce the Fourteenth Amendment with legislation that is congruent and proportional to a documented pattern of state constitutional violations; it cannot redefine the right (Boerne).
No. The Fourteenth Amendment applies only to state action (Civil Rights Cases; Morrison).

front: What federal power reaches private racial discrimination in property sales?
back: Thirteenth Amendment § 2 — badges and incidents of slavery (Jones v. Alfred H. Mayer; 42 U.S.C. § 1982). Also the Commerce Clause for businesses.

front: Why was the VRA preclearance coverage formula struck in Shelby County?
back: It burdened some states more than others based on decades-old data, violating equal sovereignty; current burdens need current needs.

A statute implementing a valid treaty is valid under the Necessary and Proper Clause even if it would otherwise exceed Article I; but treaties cannot violate individual rights (Reid v. Covert plurality).
(1) Congress authorized → maximum power; (2) Congress silent → zone of twilight; (3) contrary to Congress's will → lowest ebb, valid only if exclusive presidential power.

front: Can the President impose tariffs under IEEPA?
back: No. IEEPA's power to regulate importation does not authorize tariffs (Learning Resources v. Trump, 2026).
For agency or executive action of vast economic and political significance, clear congressional authorization is required (West Virginia v. EPA; Biden v. Nebraska).
Overruled Chevron: courts exercise independent judgment on statutory meaning; no deference to agency interpretations of ambiguous statutes (2024).
Equal rank; the later in time controls. Neither can override the Constitution.
Valid without Senate consent; preempt conflicting state law (Belmont; Pink; Garamendi); do not override a prior federal statute.

front: Is a non-self-executing treaty enforceable domestic law?
back: No — not until Congress implements it; the President cannot make it binding on state courts unilaterally (Medellín).

front: Who appoints principal vs. inferior officers?
back: Principal: President with Senate advice and consent. Inferior: Congress may vest in the President alone, courts of law, or heads of departments.
Directed and supervised by a principal officer appointed with Senate consent (Edmond); unreviewable final decisions point to principal status (Arthrex).

front: Can Congress appoint members of an agency that enforces federal law?
back: No. Officers exercising executive power must be appointed under Article II (Buckley v. Valeo).

Presumptively 10 days or more: 4–9 days is presumptively too short (only a very unusual circumstance, e.g., a national catastrophe, rebuts); 3 days or fewer never suffices. Pro forma sessions count as sessions if the Senate can transact business (Noel Canning).

front: Removal of principal executive officers after Trump v. Slaughter (2026)
back: At will. For-cause protection for FTC commissioners is unconstitutional; Humphrey's Executor overruled. Congress may not reserve a removal role (Myers; Bowsher).

For inferior officers with limited duties, removable by a principal officer for good cause (Morrison); not two layers of for-cause protection (Free Enterprise Fund). Fed governors treated as protected (Trump v. Cook, 2026).
Federal offenses only; not impeachment; may be conditional; may precede conviction; Congress cannot limit its effect.

front: Why is a legislative veto invalid?
back: Congress may take binding action only through bicameral passage and presentment (INS v. Chadha).

front: Why was the Line Item Veto Act invalid?
back: Cancelling parts of a signed statute amends law without bicameralism and presentment (Clinton v. City of New York).
If the President neither signs nor returns a bill within 10 days (Sundays excepted) and Congress's adjournment prevents return, the bill does not become law.
Congress may delegate if it lays down an intelligible principle to guide the delegee (J.W. Hampton; Whitman).
Absolute immunity from damages for acts within the outer perimeter of official duties (Nixon v. Fitzgerald); none for unofficial or pre-office conduct (Clinton v. Jones).

front: Presidential criminal immunity (Trump v. United States, 2024)
back: Absolute for core constitutional powers; at least presumptive for other official acts; none for unofficial acts.
Presumptive privilege yields to a demonstrated, specific need for evidence in a criminal trial (United States v. Nixon).

front: What does the Speech or Debate Clause protect?
back: Members and their aides from liability or questioning for legislative acts (speeches, votes, committee work). Not press releases, newsletters or taking bribes.
Absolute for judicial acts unless in clear absence of all jurisdiction (Stump); not for administrative acts (Forrester).

front: Can a state tax a federal contractor?
back: Yes, if the tax is nondiscriminatory, even if the burden passes to the U.S.; it cannot tax the U.S. directly or discriminate against it or its contractors.

front: Does the Tenth Amendment exempt states from a generally applicable federal law?
back: No (Garcia). States are protected by the political process and the anti-commandeering rule.
New York (no forcing state legislatures to regulate — take title); Printz (no conscripting state officers); Murphy (no barring states from repealing their laws).

front: DCC rule for discriminatory state laws
back: Virtually per se invalid unless the state shows a legitimate local purpose that cannot be served by reasonable nondiscriminatory alternatives (Philadelphia v. NJ; Maine v. Taylor survived).
A nondiscriminatory law is invalid only if the burden on interstate commerce is clearly excessive in relation to the putative local benefits.

When a state buys, sells or hires with its own resources it may favor residents without violating the DCC (Reeves); no downstream conditions (Wunnicke plurality); no exception under Article IV P&I (Camden).
Laws favoring a state's own public entity performing a traditional governmental function are not discriminatory under the DCC.

front: Complete Auto test for state taxes
back: Substantial nexus (no physical presence needed — Wayfair); fair apportionment; nondiscrimination; fair relation to state services.
Express; implied field (pervasive scheme or dominant federal interest); implied conflict (impossibility or obstacle to congressional purposes).

front: Can a state impose stricter rules than federal law?
back: Yes, unless federal law expressly preempts, occupies the field, or the stricter rule conflicts.

front: Can Congress authorize discriminatory state laws?
back: Yes, as to the dormant Commerce Clause, if unmistakably clear (Prudential v. Benjamin). Not violations of equal protection (Met Life v. Ward) or the right to travel (Saenz).

front: Article IV Privileges and Immunities test
back: State discrimination against out-of-state individuals regarding fundamental rights (livelihood) is invalid unless a substantial reason exists and the discrimination bears a substantial relationship to it.

front: Who can invoke Article IV P&I?
back: Only individual U.S. citizens — not corporations or aliens.

Private conduct is state action if it performs a function traditionally and exclusively reserved to the state (elections — Terry; company town — Marsh). Not utilities, schools, nursing homes, cable access.
Judicial enforcement of racial covenants (Shelley); symbiotic lessee (Burton); joint action (Lugar); entwinement (Brentwood); peremptory strikes (Edmonson).

front: Lindke v. Freed test for officials' social media
back: State action only if the official (1) had actual authority to speak for the state on the matter and (2) purported to exercise it in the posts.

front: Which Bill of Rights guarantees are NOT incorporated?
back: Fifth Amendment grand-jury indictment (Hurtado); Seventh Amendment civil jury; Third Amendment never decided.

front: What is a property interest for procedural due process?
back: A legitimate claim of entitlement from an independent source (statute, contract, mutual understanding) — Roth; Sindermann. Not a unilateral expectation or at-will job.
(1) Private interest affected; (2) risk of erroneous deprivation and value of additional safeguards; (3) government's interest, including burdens.
Tenured public employee: pre-termination notice, explanation of the evidence and an opportunity to respond, then a full post-termination hearing.
Welfare termination needs a pre-termination evidentiary hearing (Goldberg); disability benefits can be cut with a post-termination hearing (Mathews).
Carefully describe the asserted right; it is fundamental only if deeply rooted in the Nation's history and tradition and implicit in ordered liberty (reaffirmed in Dobbs).

front: List the recognized fundamental rights under substantive due process
back: Marry; procreate; contraception; family living arrangements; parental care, custody and upbringing; private intimate conduct; (assumed) refusing medical treatment; travel; vote; arms.

front: Standard for abortion regulation after Dobbs
back: Rational basis; no federal constitutional right to abortion.
Reprehensibility; ratio to compensatory damages (single-digit presumptively); comparable civil penalties (Gore; State Farm).

front: Three components of the right to travel (Saenz)
back: Enter and leave another state; be treated as a welcome visitor (Art. IV P&I); new permanent residents treated like other citizens (14th Am. P or I).

If the Second Amendment's text covers the conduct, it is presumptively protected; the government must show the law is consistent with the Nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation. No means-end scrutiny.
Analogues need not be historical twins; the law must be consistent with the principles (how and why) of the tradition. Temporary disarmament of a person found to be a credible threat is valid.
Strict (gov't: necessary to compelling interest); intermediate (gov't: substantially related to important interest); rational basis (challenger: no rational relation to any legitimate interest).

front: Is disparate impact enough for strict scrutiny?
back: No. Need discriminatory purpose — 'because of, not in spite of' (Davis; Feeney; Arlington Heights factors).

front: Arlington Heights factors for discriminatory purpose
back: Disparate impact; historical background; sequence of events; departures from normal procedures or substance; legislative or administrative history.

front: Standard for benign racial classifications (affirmative action)
back: Strict scrutiny (Adarand; Croson). Remedying the entity's own identified discrimination can be compelling; societal discrimination is not. SFFA (2023): race-conscious admissions invalid.
Race as the predominant factor in drawing district lines → strict scrutiny (Shaw; Miller). Partisan gerrymandering is nonjusticiable (Rucho).
Strict scrutiny, except political-function jobs (police, teachers, probation officers, jurors) → rational basis. Federal alienage rules → rational basis.
Intermediate scrutiny with an exceedingly persuasive justification: important objective, substantially related means, no stereotypes (VMI). Government's burden.
Ban on certain treatments for minors' gender dysphoria classifies by age and medical use, not sex → rational basis; upheld.

front: Standard for classifications against nonmarital children
back: Intermediate scrutiny (Clark v. Jeter).

front: Which classes get only rational basis?
back: Age, disability, wealth, economic interests, (federally) sexual orientation — but animus fails (Moreno, Cleburne, Romer, Windsor).

front: Is education a fundamental right under federal equal protection?
back: No (Rodriguez); but a total denial to undocumented children required substantial justification (Plyler).

(1) Permanent physical occupation or government-authorized physical appropriation/access (Loretto; Cedar Point); (2) deprivation of all economically beneficial use (Lucas), absent a nuisance/property-law exception.
(1) Economic impact on the owner; (2) interference with distinct investment-backed expectations; (3) character of the government action.
Essential nexus (Nollan) + rough proportionality by individualized determination (Dolan); applies to denials and money (Koontz) and legislative conditions (Sheetz).
Any rational public purpose, including economic development under a comprehensive plan.

front: Temporary takings and when to sue
back: Compensation owed for the period (First English); owner may sue a local government under § 1983 immediately without state litigation (Knick); a State is not a § 1983 person (Will) so sue it in state court.

State law substantially impairing an existing contract is valid only if drawn in an appropriate and reasonable way to advance a significant and legitimate public purpose; less deference for the state's own contracts.

front: Calder v. Bull ex post facto categories
back: Retroactively (1) criminalizing innocent conduct, (2) aggravating a crime, (3) increasing punishment, (4) easing proof for conviction. Criminal/punitive laws only.
Legislative act + specifically identified persons + punishment + no judicial trial.
Government may define the limits of the program it funds (Rust) but may not require recipients to adopt its views outside the program (AOSI).

front: Fourteenth Amendment Privileges or Immunities — what it protects
back: Only rights of national citizenship (Slaughter-House), notably new residents' right to equal treatment (Saenz).
A neutral law of general applicability burdening religion needs only a rational basis.

front: When does strict scrutiny apply in free exercise?
back: When the law is not neutral (targets religion or shows hostility — Lukumi, Masterpiece) or not generally applicable (individualized exemptions — Fulton; comparable secular activity treated better — Tandon).

front: Can a state exclude religious schools from a neutral aid program?
back: No — status or use exclusions trigger strict scrutiny (Trinity Lutheran; Espinoza; Carson). Exception: funding clergy training (Locke v. Davey).
Religious organizations' selection of ministers (employees with key religious functions) is beyond employment-discrimination law (Hosanna-Tabor; Our Lady of Guadalupe).
RFRA: federal government; RLUIPA: state land use and institutionalized persons. Both: substantial burden → compelling interest + least restrictive means.
Historical practices and understandings; no coercion (Kennedy v. Bremerton, 2022). Lemon abandoned.

front: Is graduation prayer by clergy constitutional?
back: No — coercive for students (Lee v. Weisman). Legislative prayer is valid by tradition (Marsh; Town of Greece).
Laws preferring some religions over others get strict scrutiny (Larson); line based on religious practice or theology fails (Catholic Charities, 2025).
Applies to speech because of its topic, message, function or purpose; or is facially neutral but justified by reference to content or adopted for disagreement with the message.
Government must prove the law is narrowly tailored — least restrictive means — to a compelling interest.
Content-neutral; narrowly tailored to a significant government interest (no substantially more burden than necessary); ample alternative channels.
Traditional and designated: content-based → strict; neutral → TPM. Limited and nonpublic: reasonable and viewpoint-neutral.
History of the medium communicating government messages; public perception that the government speaks; government's active control (Summum; Walker; Shurtleff).
Advocacy directed to inciting or producing imminent lawless action and likely to incite or produce it.
At least recklessness: the speaker consciously disregarded a substantial risk the communication would be viewed as threatening violence.
Personally abusive words, face-to-face, likely to provoke an immediate violent reaction (Chaplinsky); no viewpoint discrimination within the category (R.A.V.).

(1) Average person, contemporary community standards, prurient interest; (2) patently offensive sexual conduct specifically defined by law; (3) lacks serious literary, artistic, political or scientific value (national reasonable-person standard).
Actual malice — knowledge of falsity or reckless disregard — proven by clear and convincing evidence (NYT v. Sullivan).
Lawful and not misleading? → substantial interest → directly advances → not more extensive than necessary (reasonable fit).

Schools may restrict student speech only on a reasonable forecast of substantial disruption or invasion of others' rights. Exceptions: lewd (Fraser), school-sponsored (Hazelwood), drug promotion (Morse); off-campus diminished (Mahanoy).
Citizen speech (not pursuant to official duties — Garcetti) + matter of public concern (Connick) → Pickering balance → Mt. Healthy same-decision defense.
Unconstitutional unless party affiliation is an appropriate requirement for the job (policymaking or confidential) — Elrod; Branti; Rutan.
Only for knowing membership with specific intent to further the group's illegal aims (Scales; Baird; Wadmond).
Within government power; furthers important interest; interest unrelated to suppression of expression; incidental restriction no greater than essential.
Intent to convey a particularized message + great likelihood viewers understand it.
Heavy presumption against prior restraints; permit schemes need narrow, objective, definite standards (no unbridled discretion); content-based licensing needs Freedman safeguards.
Must obey a court injunction until it is vacated, even if unconstitutional (Walker v. Birmingham); a facially void licensing statute may be ignored (Shuttlesworth).

Vague: person of ordinary intelligence cannot tell what is prohibited, or arbitrary enforcement invited. Overbroad: clear but reaches a substantial amount of protected speech relative to legitimate sweep.

front: Does the press have a privilege to refuse a grand-jury subpoena?
back: No First Amendment privilege (Branzburg). California shield law gives immunity from contempt (Cal. Const. art. I, § 2(b)).
Presumptively open; closure needs an overriding interest, specific findings, narrow tailoring; no mandatory closure statutes (Globe; Press-Enterprise).

front: Compelled disclosure of members or donors
back: Exacting scrutiny: substantial relation to a sufficiently important interest + narrow tailoring (NAACP v. Alabama; AFP v. Bonta).
Expressive group may exclude members whose presence significantly burdens its message (Dale); large, unselective clubs cannot (Roberts; Rotary).

Expenditure limits → strict scrutiny (Buckley; Citizens United); contribution limits → closely drawn to quid pro quo corruption; disclosure → exacting scrutiny. Party coordinated-expenditure limits invalid (NRSC v. FEC, 2026).

front: Government pressure on intermediaries (NRA v. Vullo, 2024)
back: Officials may not coerce private parties to punish or suppress a third party's speech; persuasion is permitted.
Compelled labor through physical or legal coercion; excepts criminal punishment and civic duties (draft, jury, road work — Butler v. Perry). Applies to private actors.

front: Citizenship Clause after Trump v. Barbara (2026)
back: Children born in the U.S. are citizens even if parents are unlawfully or temporarily present (Wong Kim Ark); EO 14160 invalid.
Purposeful race-based denial or abridgment of the vote (Mobile v. Bolden plurality); ancestry as proxy for race counts (Rice v. Cayetano).

front: Turner v. Safley test for prison regulations
back: Reasonably related to legitimate penological interests: rational connection; alternative means; impact of accommodation; absence of ready alternatives. Race → strict scrutiny (Johnson v. California).
Likely success on the merits; likely irreparable harm without relief; balance of equities favors plaintiff; public interest.
State officials in personal capacity; local governments for their policies or customs (Monell). Not states or state officials sued for damages in official capacity (Will).
